subject: Version Control Systems

assessmentTargets.concept: Recognize that Git is a distributed version control system used to track project changes
assessmentTargets.supportingEvidence: Git is basically a distributed version control system, which will be helping the developers to keep track about whatever changes they are doing in the project that they are developing.
assessmentTargets.evidenceSpan: Git is basically a distributed version control system, which will be helping the developers to keep track about whatever changes they are doing in the project that they are developing.
assessmentTargets.instruction: Explain in your own words what a distributed version control system is and why it is useful.

assessmentTargets.concept: State the purpose of the `git --version` command
assessmentTargets.supportingEvidence: So the first command you have is Git version. So if you want to know if the Git is installed in your system, then we will be using this particular command called as Git version.
assessmentTargets.evidenceSpan: So the first command you have is Git version. ... if you want to know if the Git is installed in your system, then we will be using this particular command called as Git version.
assessmentTargets.instruction: Provide the exact command and describe what information it returns.

assessmentTargets.concept: Identify the two pieces of user information required by `git config --global` and how to set them
assessmentTargets.supportingEvidence: You have to give your details like your username, your email ID... you have to give git config --global user.name "..." and user.email "..."
assessmentTargets.evidenceSpan: ...you have to give git config --global user.name "..." and user.email "..."
assessmentTargets.instruction: Write the two commands needed to set your name and email globally.

assessmentTargets.concept: Explain what `git init` does and what message it returns
assessmentTargets.supportingEvidence: When you use git init, it will tell you that an empty repository has been created.
assessmentTargets.evidenceSpan: When you use git init, it will tell you that an empty repository has been created.
assessmentTargets.instruction: Run `git init` in a new folder and note the output message.

assessmentTargets.concept: Describe the information provided by `git status` regarding staged and unstaged changes
assessmentTargets.supportingEvidence: It will tell you what are the changes you have made and which changes have not yet been saved into the repository.
assessmentTargets.evidenceSpan: It will tell you what are the changes you have made and which changes have not yet been saved into the repository.
assessmentTargets.instruction: List the sections shown by `git status` and explain their meaning.

reserveTargets.concept: Explain the role of the `--global` flag in `git config`
reserveTargets.supportingEvidence: you have to give git config --global user.name "..."
reserveTargets.evidenceSpan: you have to give git config --global user.name "..."
reserveTargets.instruction: Describe how `--global` affects the scope of the configuration.

reserveTargets.concept: Interpret what an “empty repository” means after running `git init`
reserveTargets.supportingEvidence: it will tell you that an empty repository has been created
reserveTargets.evidenceSpan: it will tell you that an empty repository has been created
reserveTargets.instruction: Explain why the repository is initially empty.

reserveTargets.concept: Differentiate between changes that are saved (committed) and those not yet saved as reported by `git status`
reserveTargets.supportingEvidence: which changes have not yet been saved into the repository
reserveTargets.evidenceSpan: which changes have not yet been saved into the repository
reserveTargets.instruction: Identify which listed files need to be added or committed.
